Domaine Bonnigal-Bodet
Limeray, Touraine-Amboise — Loire Valley

Certified Organic
Long time best friends Jean-Baptiste Bonnigal and Stéphane Bodet first cut their teeth in the industry in Saint-Émilion. After getting their diplomas, Stéphane stayed in Saint-Émilion, while Jean-Baptiste headed to New Zealand and Australia.
JB eventually returned to his native Loire and spent several years working with François Chidaine in Montlouis-sur-Loire. He remains closely tied to the Chidaine family as he is married to François' daughter. In 2016, he took over his family estate in Amboise and invited Stéphane to join him in the project.
From the get-go, the two friends were aligned in their vision in making wines with purity and precision as well as their commitment to farming organically and biodynamically. Their farming practices including hoeing every two weeks to aerate the soil and encourage microbial life, treating the vines only as required, thinning leaves, and harvesting manually. Fermentations are always with native yeasts and with their sparkling wines, tirage is done at the domaine.

2496 Malbec 2024 13 6 MAN MEETS MOUNTAIN, MENDOZA “Great things are done when men and mountains meet; this is not done by jostling in the street”. The quest for higher quality has seen Argentina’s most ambitious winemakers push into the Andes foothills, where the higher altitude and meagre soils produce the finest grapes. Man Meets Mountain celebrates those that face up to the challenges posed by nature with a Malbec packed full of blueberry, blackcurrant and plum.
2147 Malbec 2024 13 6 MANOS NEGRAS Alejandro Sejanovich is arguably Argentina’s most knowledgeable viticulturist. Having worked as vineyard director for Bodega Catena Zapata for 16 years, he pioneered high-altitude vineyard planting and conducted ground-breaking research into Mendoza’s Malbec clones. With Manos Negras, Alejandro combines his love of minerality and altitude with a magical touch in the winery to produce some of the region’s most terroir-driven wines. Not only altitude but also latitude play a part in the wines from Manos Negras all capturing the spirit of Manos Negras through a myriad of soil types and grape expressions.

Domaine de l’Austral | Saumur-Puy Notre Dame
Certified Organic
While working on a farm in Australia, Pauline Mourrain and Laurent Troubat had their “A-ha!” moment that their calling was to work on an organic vineyard and make wine. While Pauline was interning with Aimeric Mélaric, she met Françoise and Philippe Gourdon of Chteau Tour Grise, who were retiring soon and in search of young talent to take over their historic estate. (read more)
Saumur-Champigny
Sylvain Dittière - La Porte Saint Jean |Montreuil-Bellay
Certified Organic
Sylvain Dittière learned how to cultivate plants in his youth. His parents were rose growers. But as lovely as roses may be, they left him uninspired, and so he decidedly turned to the vine and began an apprenticeship at Domaine du Collier, Antoine Foucault’s iconic organic domaine in Saumur. It was here that Sylvain’s passion for making wines without chemical interventions took root. He went on to complete his studies in oenology while simultaneously challenging much of what he learned in school while interning at yet another benchmark organic domaine in Saumur – Thierry Germain’s Domaine des Roches Neuves. To round out his education, or “un-education” as Sylvain puts it, he followed up with stints at two more well-regarded organic domaines in opposite corners of France – two years alongside Marc Tempé in Alsace, and then another year with Gerard Gauby in the Roussillon, principally in the cellar. All in all, a very impressive “un-education!” (read more)

Côteaux du Giennois
Florian Roblin |Maimbry
Certified Organic
Often referred to as “the poor man’s Sancerre,” the Côteaux du Giennois lies approximately 20 km north of Sancerre. The best parcels, such as Florian’s ‘Champ Gibault,’ often have a mix of clay and flint over a chalk base. This all translates to affordable wines with a clear cut mineral character. His whites could easily be mistaken for Sancerre tasted blind, and his red offers a bit more richness, structure, and fruit-forwardness than many Sancerre rouges – all at the fraction of the price. (read more)
Pouilly-sur-Loire / Pouilly-Fumé
Jonathan Pabiot | Pouilly-sur-Loire
Certified Organic & Biodynamic
In 2005, after working with Léon Barral in the Languedoc, 4th generation winegrower Jonathan returned to his family estate, convinced that organic farming was the way to go. His father, however, was not easily convinced and gave him just 1.5ha to start. Jonathan then acquired an additional 1.5ha and converted all 3 to organic farming. A few years later, when his father saw how sought after his son’s cuvées became, he joined forces with Jonathan and allowed him to convert the remaining 17ha of the family vineyards to organic. It wasn’t long until Jonathan saw a dramatic improvement and felt that practicing biodynamics would be the natural next step. (read more)
Loiret
Julien Thurel (cider) | Loury
Certified Organic
Julien Thurel, a woodsman and ornithologist, has been making foraged and organically farmed pear and apple ciders since 2012. This bird and tree specialist has devoted much time to researching local apple and pear varieties and selecting the ones best suited to his native clay, limestone, and silex soils. A perfectionist and nativist, Julien is driven by a mission to find the best local varieties that would lead to delicate yet aromatically complex and ageworthy ciders. (read more)

Serve each style at its best: most whites are served too cold and most reds too warm.
Style,Temp,Tip
Sparkling,6–8°C / 43–46°F,Chill about 3 hours
Light white & rosé,7–10°C / 45–50°F,Fridge for 2–3 hours
Full white,10–13°C / 50–55°F,Take out 20 minutes early
Light red,12–14°C / 54–57°F,Brief chill helps
Full red,15–18°C / 59–64°F,Cooler than room temp

Typical times once opened, stoppered and stored cold. Taste before pouring: the wine is fine as long as it still tastes fresh to you.
| Style | Keeps for | Tip |
---
| Sparkling | 1–3 days | Use a proper sparkling-wine stopper; the bubbles fade fast. |
| Light white and rosé | 3–5 days | Recork and keep in the fridge. |
| Full-bodied white | 3–5 days | Fridge; oaked whites lose freshness a little sooner. |
| Light red | 2–3 days | Fridge, then take it out 30 minutes before pouring. |
| Full red | 3–5 days | Fridge too: cold slows the air's effect. Warm it up before serving. |
| Sweet wine | 3–7 days | Sugar helps it keep; store in the fridge. |
| Fino and Manzanilla Sherry | 2–3 days | Treat it like a white wine: fridge, and drink it fresh. |
| Ruby port, Madeira and tawny port | Weeks | Ruby and LBV keep a few weeks; tawny and Madeira, a month or more. |
To make it last: recork straight after pouring, keep the bottle upright, and pour leftovers into a smaller bottle so less air touches the wine.
The shape of the bowl changes how the wine smells and how it reaches your mouth. One good all-purpose glass with a tulip-shaped bowl works for almost everything.
Champagne names, with the number of standard 75 cl bottles and 125 ml glasses each one holds. In Bordeaux a 3-litre bottle is called a Double Magnum, a 5-litre a Jeroboam and a 6-litre an Imperial.
The label word tells you how much sugar is in the bottle, in grams per litre, mostly from the dosage added just before corking. The same EU terms are used for Champagne, Cava, Crémant, Prosecco, Franciacorta and Sekt.
Also Pas dosé or Dosage zéro: no sugar added. Bone dry, very crisp and pure.
Very dry, with a sharp, almost salty freshness.
Dry. The most common style: crisp, with just enough sugar to soften the acidity.
Off-dry, with a soft touch of sweetness. Many Proseccos are made this way.
Noticeably sweet, despite the name.
Sweet. Good with fruit tarts and lightly sweet desserts.
Very sweet, a dessert style; rare today.
Driest at the top. Ranges overlap a little because the rules allow a small margin. High acidity hides sugar, so a Brut with 10 g/L of residual sugar still tastes dry; for comparison, cola has about 106 g/L.
Most bottles are fine, but these are the faults worth knowing. In a restaurant, mention it to the sommelier straight away; a shop will usually replace a faulty bottle if most of it is left.
| Fault | Smells or looks like | Cause | Return it? |
------|
| Corked | Damp cardboard, musty cellar, wet dog; the fruit seems muted | A compound called TCA, often from the cork | Yes |
| Oxidised | Bruised apple, nutty or sherry-like; whites turn golden-brown | Too much air, in the winery or after a bad seal | Yes, unless the style is meant to taste like that (e.g. Sherry, tawny port) |
| Reduced | Struck match, rotten egg, cabbage | Sulphur compounds from too little air during winemaking | Swirl or decant first; often it clears in minutes. Return it if it doesn't |
| Heat-damaged | Jammy, stewed or flat fruit; the cork may be pushed up or sticky | Stored or shipped too warm | Yes |
| Brettanomyces (Brett) | Farmyard, sticking plaster, smoky or medicinal | A wild yeast | A little is a matter of taste; return it if it dominates |
| Volatile acidity | Nail-varnish remover or vinegar | Acetic bacteria | Yes, if it is strong |
Not faults: little crystals (tartrates, sometimes called wine diamonds), sediment in older reds, or a slight prickle in some young whites.
Weather shapes each harvest. Ratings and drinking windows are broad, simplified summaries of the general view as of today, not verdicts on any single bottle. Producer and wine level matter as much as the year.

Quiz yourself on the regions, grapes and producers in this guide, then review a tasting framework.
A systematic, exam-style approach: describe the wine, assess its quality, then draw your conclusions. The analysis below checks your reasoning against this guide.
Add a photo of the bottle or label. It prints on the tasting sheet.
High acidity, lower alcohol: often a cooler climate.
Low acidity, high alcohol, ripe fruit: often a warmer climate.
Pale colour, high acidity, low tannin in a red: think Pinot Noir or Nebbiolo-like styles.
Deep colour, high tannin, full body: think Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah or Tempranillo.
Use clues as a starting point and weigh them together. No single clue decides the answer.

This guide brings together wine grapes, regions, tasting tools and study material for wine lovers and aspiring sommeliers.

A trip to the Left Bank of Bordeaux to visit two of Pauillac's First Growths from the 1855 classification, Château Mouton Rothschild and Château Lafite Rothschild, along with a tasting from Edmond de Rothschild Heritage and a drive through Margaux.
At Mouton I walked the vineyards. At Lafite the highlight was the circular barrel cellar, where the barrels sit in rings around a forest of columns, and a soil map that shows why this gravel is so good for Cabernet Sauvignon. The Edmond de Rothschild Heritage tasting, in a room lined with back-lit bottles, crossed to the Right Bank, with wines from the Saint-Émilion satellites Montagne and Puisseguin. If you want to read more, see Bordeaux and Cabernet Sauvignon.
